explanations.answer: Claiming to be Christ and a King
explanations.explanation: That's the third charge, friend. The council says they found this man "proclaiming Himself to be Christ, a King" (Luke 23:2). It sits right next to the other two charges they bring to Pilate, the Roman governor. Three accusations in one breath, and not a witness in sight yet.

Not here, friend. In Luke 23:2 the council's charges are subverting the nation, forbidding taxes to Caesar, and proclaiming Himself to be Christ, a King. Sabbath talk doesn't make their list in front of Pilate. I think I'd have gotten that one mixed up too, because it's easy to blend charges together.

That one doesn't show up in this list, friend. The council's last charge in Luke 23:2 is that He was "proclaiming Himself to be Christ, a King." They also say He was subverting the nation and forbidding taxes to Caesar, Rome's emperor. Those are the accusations laid in front of Pilate.
Close, but listen to what Jesus actually says. Pilate asks, "Are You the King of the Jews?" and Jesus replies, "You have said so." (Luke 23:3). That's not a denial. Jesus doesn't say no.
Right, friend. Pilate does ask, "Are You the King of the Jews?" But Jesus doesn't deny it. He answers, "You have said so." (Luke 23:3). Pilate walks away from that answer and turns to the crowd.

explanations.answer: He finds no basis for a charge
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Pilate says to the chief priests and the crowds, "I find no basis for a charge against this man." (Luke 23:4). The governor looks at the whole pile of accusations and comes up empty. That's a pretty big statement from the man who decides the case.

explanations.answer: He wants more time to decide
explanations.explanation: Pilate doesn't ask for more time, friend. He says plainly, "I find no basis for a charge against this man." (Luke 23:4). His mind is made up on that point right away. No waiting, no stalling.

He doesn't call for anybody else, friend. Pilate says, "I find no basis for a charge against this man." (Luke 23:4). That's his verdict, and he says it straight to the chief priests and the crowds. No witness list needed.
Yes, baker! The accusers say, "He began in Galilee and has come all the way here." (Luke 23:5). That one word matters in what happens next. I like to think Pilate's ears perked up right there.
Samaria isn't named here, friend. The accusers say Jesus "began in Galilee and has come all the way here." (Luke 23:5). The word Galilee is the one Pilate picks up on.

Egypt is a long way off from this scene, friend. In Luke 23:5 the accusers say, "He began in Galilee and has come all the way here." Galilee is the place they name, and it matters for what Pilate does next.

That's right! Once Pilate learns Jesus is under Herod's jurisdiction, he sends Him to Herod (Luke 23:7). This is Herod, the ruler of Galilee, who happens to be in Jerusalem at that time. Perfect timing for a man who wanted this case off his desk.

Caesar does come up, but only in the charges. The council said Jesus was forbidding payment of taxes to Caesar (Luke 23:2). When Pilate learns Jesus is under Herod's jurisdiction, he sends Him to Herod (Luke 23:7). Caesar, Rome's emperor, is never part of that trip.

Not yet, friend. Luke 23:7 says Pilate learns Jesus is under Herod's jurisdiction and sends Him to Herod. Pilate does say he finds no basis for a charge (Luke 23:4), but he doesn't send Him home. He passes Him along.

Yes, baker. Herod had heard about Jesus and was "hoping to see Him perform a miracle." (Luke 23:8). He had wanted to see Him for a long time. I think he showed up like a man at a magic show waiting for the main act.

Rebellion is what Pilate mentions in Luke 23:14, when he reminds them of the charge that Jesus was inciting the people to rebellion. That isn't what Herod is hoping for. Luke 23:8 says he was "hoping to see Him perform a miracle."

Herod isn't waiting for a sermon, friend. Luke 23:8 says he had heard about Jesus and "was hoping to see Him perform a miracle." That's what had him excited. He had wanted to see Jesus for a long time.

True, baker. Herod "questioned Jesus at great length, but He gave no answer." (Luke 23:9). Question after question and Jesus says nothing. I'd have filled that quiet by talking too much, and I'd have regretted it.
Not quite, friend. Luke 23:9 says Herod "questioned Jesus at great length, but He gave no answer." Jesus doesn't answer him at all. All that questioning gets silence back.
They're not quiet, friend. Luke 23:10 says the chief priests and scribes stood there, "vehemently accusing Him." While Herod questions, they keep the accusations coming. The text calls it vehement.
Right, baker. The chief priests and scribes do stand there, but Luke 23:10 says they were "vehemently accusing Him." Nothing quiet about it. Herod is asking questions and they're loudly piling on.

That's it, baker. Luke 23:12 says, "That day Herod and Pilate became friends; before this time they had been enemies." Two rulers who couldn't stand each other end up friends in one day. That's a strange way for a friendship to start.
They weren't strangers, friend. Luke 23:12 says "before this time they had been enemies." Herod and Pilate knew each other well enough to be at odds. Then that very day they became friends.
Partners is a nice thought, but no. Luke 23:12 says "before this time they had been enemies." They only became friends that day. Before that, they were on opposite sides.
Pilate says the opposite, friend. He tells them he examined Jesus in their presence and found Him "not guilty of your charges against Him." (Luke 23:14). He says it right to their faces.

Yes, baker. Pilate says he has examined Jesus in their presence and found Him "not guilty of your charges against Him." (Luke 23:14). He's talking to the same crowd that brought the charges. He doesn't find Jesus guilty.

True, baker. Pilate says, "Neither has Herod, for he sent Him back to us." (Luke 23:15). So the governor and the ruler of Galilee have both looked at this case. Neither one lands where the accusers want.
Not so, friend. Pilate says, "Neither has Herod, for he sent Him back to us." (Luke 23:15). That means Herod didn't find Jesus guilty of their charges either. Pilate points to it as part of his case.
Yes, baker. Pilate says, "Therefore I will punish Him and release Him." (Luke 23:16). Release is the word he lands on. The text gives us his plan and that's all it gives.
Prison isn't in his plan, friend. Pilate says, "Therefore I will punish Him and release Him." (Luke 23:16). The word is release. The only man headed to prison in this story is the one already there.
He's done questioning, friend. Pilate has already examined Jesus (Luke 23:14). His plan in Luke 23:16 is, "Therefore I will punish Him and release Him." The word he uses is release.
That's him, baker. They cry out, "Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!" (Luke 23:18). They all say it in unison. It's a loud swap they're asking for.
Malchus isn't in this scene, friend. He's the high priest's servant, named in John 18:10. In Luke 23:18 they shout, "Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!" Barabbas is the name they call out.

Zacchaeus is a different man, friend. He was a chief tax collector who climbed a tree to see Jesus (Luke 19:2-4). In Luke 23:18 the cry is, "Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!" That's the name they shout.

Yes, baker. Luke 23:19 says Barabbas "had been imprisoned for an insurrection in the city, and for murder." It's a heavy detail, and the text puts it right there. These are the charges against the man they want freed.

Blasphemy isn't what the text says about him, friend. Luke 23:19 says Barabbas "had been imprisoned for an insurrection in the city, and for murder." It's a heavy part of the story. Murder is the other charge.
Nothing about the temple here, friend. Luke 23:19 says Barabbas "had been imprisoned for an insurrection in the city, and for murder." It's a heavy detail. Murder is the other reason he's in prison.
That's what they shout, baker. Luke 23:21 says, "they kept shouting, 'Crucify Him! Crucify Him!'" Pilate wants to release Jesus and they won't hear it. This is a hard part of the story.
Not what the text records, friend. In Luke 23:21 they "kept shouting, 'Crucify Him! Crucify Him!'" Pilate is trying to release Jesus, and that's the answer he gets back. It's a heavy moment.
Banishing isn't mentioned, friend. Luke 23:21 says they "kept shouting, 'Crucify Him! Crucify Him!'" Pilate wants to release Jesus and that's what he's shouted back at. It's a hard thing to read.

That's right. Luke 23:23 says they were "demanding with loud voices for Jesus to be crucified. And their clamor prevailed." Pilate said release over and over. In the end the noise won. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story.
His verdict doesn't win, friend. Pilate said he found Jesus not guilty and planned to release Him (Luke 23:14-16). But Luke 23:23 says "their clamor prevailed." The shouting won out.
Herod doesn't get a final word here, friend. He already sent Jesus back to Pilate (Luke 23:11). What wins out in Luke 23:23 is that "their clamor prevailed." It's the shouting of the crowd.

explanations.answer: Sentences that their demand be met
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Luke 23:24 says, "So Pilate sentenced that their demand be met." He had said again and again that he found no offense worthy of death. In the end, he gave them what they were demanding. It's a heavy moment in the story.

He doesn't release both, friend. Luke 23:25 says he released the one imprisoned for insurrection and murder, and handed Jesus over to their will. Releasing both would've changed the whole story. Luke 23:24 says he "sentenced that their demand be met."

explanations.answer: Calls for a brand new hearing
explanations.explanation: No new hearing, friend. Luke 23:24 says, "So Pilate sentenced that their demand be met." The clamor had prevailed and he went with their demand. It ends there for now.
True, baker. Luke 23:25 says, "As they had requested, he released the one imprisoned for insurrection and murder." That's Barabbas, and he's freed because of what they asked for. It's a heavy moment.

It's true, friend. Luke 23:25 says, "As they had requested, he released the one imprisoned for insurrection and murder, and he handed Jesus over to their will." That's Barabbas going free. It's a heavy part of the story.
